stories.title: Police Nab Woman Linked to Sneaky Coffee Money Scheme
stories.headline_kid: A 49-year-old woman was arrested in Singapore for allegedly helping run a coffee-themed investment scheme that police say tricks people out of their money.
summary: On Thursday, Singapore police arrested a 49-year-old woman for her alleged role in promoting an investment scheme linked to a platform called Fun Coffee. The platform is connected to a chain of cafes and is said to be based in Vietnam.

Police say Fun Coffee looks like a pyramid-selling scheme. This means people are promised big rewards not just for investing money, but for getting their friends and family to join too - much like a chain letter that only really benefits the people at the very top.

The problem with these schemes is that they cannot last forever. Eventually, there are not enough new people joining, and most participants - especially those who joined later - end up losing their money instead of earning it.

Police are continuing their investigation and have reminded the public to be extra careful with any investment that promises quick, easy profits. If something sounds too exciting to be true, it usually is.

lenses.me: If someone ever tells you that you'll get rich just by getting your friends to join something, that's a big warning sign - just like this Fun Coffee scheme.
lenses.family: Parents and grandparents are often the ones targeted by investment tricks, so it helps to check with a trusted adult before putting money into anything that seems amazing.
lenses.friends: If a friend mentions an app promising easy money, you could be the sensible one who says, 'Let's find out more before we trust it.'
lenses.nation: Singapore's police work hard to catch people running scams so that everyone's hard-earned savings stay safe.
lenses.world: This scheme was run from Vietnam but reached people in Singapore, showing how easily online money tricks can cross borders.

stories.title: Top Honours for Chief Justice and Trusted Advisor Ahead of National Day
stories.headline_kid: Just before National Day, Singapore gave its highest award for citizens to Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon and former advisor Eddie Teo.
summary: Every year around National Day, Singapore hands out awards to people who have served the country well. This year, 7,491 people were recognised - 6,624 of them ordinary citizens and 867 from the military.

Among them, two men received the country's highest civilian honour: Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon and Mr Eddie Teo, who used to chair the Council of Presidential Advisers. A Chief Justice is like the country's top judge, making sure the law is applied fairly to everyone.
The Council of Presidential Advisers helps guide important decisions the President makes, so Mr Teo's role was also very important behind the scenes for many years.
These awards are Singapore's way of saying 'thank you' to people - from top leaders to everyday volunteers - who have worked hard for the good of the nation.

lenses.me: It shows that years of hard work and dedication, even quiet work behind the scenes, can be recognised and celebrated.
lenses.family: Your family might spot familiar community leaders, like grassroots volunteers or teachers, among the thousands being honoured this year.
lenses.friends: You and your friends could talk about which everyday heroes in your own neighbourhood deserve an award too.
lenses.nation: The awards celebrate people who help keep Singapore fair, safe and running smoothly, from judges to soldiers.
lenses.world: Many countries have similar national honours, showing that valuing people who serve their community is something shared around the world.

stories.title: Two Men Charged Over Lawyer's Secret Escape Plan
stories.headline_kid: Two men are now facing charges in court for allegedly helping a lawyer sneak out of Singapore without going through proper checks.
summary: Lawyer Lim Tean was supposed to surrender himself in Singapore to serve a jail sentence, but he did not show up. He was later arrested by Malaysian police in Johor Bahru, just across the border.

On Saturday, two Singaporean men - aged 37 and 44 - were charged in court for allegedly arranging for Lim Tean to leave Singapore illegally, meaning he did not go through the normal checkpoint with proper passport checks.
Leaving a country without going through official checks is against the law, even for a short trip across the Causeway. Helping someone avoid serving their punishment is also treated very seriously.
This case reminds everyone that rules like border checks exist for good reason, and that no one - not even a lawyer who knows the law well - is above following it.

lenses.me: It's a reminder that everyone must follow rules, even grown-ups, and that the law applies fairly to all of us.
lenses.family: Whenever your family crosses the Causeway to Johor Bahru, you go through immigration checks - this case shows exactly why those checks matter.
lenses.friends: You could discuss with classmates why it isn't fair for anyone to dodge rules that everyone else has to follow.
lenses.nation: Singapore's justice system depends on people following the law, even when it's inconvenient, and this case shows authorities take that seriously.
lenses.world: Singapore and Malaysia work closely together on cross-border matters like this, since our two countries share a border and cooperate on keeping it safe.

stories.title: Typhoon Dolphin Slams Japan's Okinawa Islands
stories.headline_kid: A powerful typhoon called Dolphin hit Japan's Okinawa islands with very strong winds, while China closed its ports to prepare for the same storm.
summary: Typhoon Dolphin struck Japan's southern Okinawa prefecture on Saturday, with winds blowing as fast as 162km/h and gusts reaching a huge 216km/h. That's faster than an MRT train zooming at top speed!

The typhoon injured five people, mostly elderly residents who fell in the strong winds, and cut off electricity to about 14,000 buildings. Across the sea, China shut down ports and stopped ferries to prepare for the storm's arrival on its east coast.

A typhoon is basically a giant spinning storm that forms over warm ocean water, similar to a hurricane. Countries like Japan and the Philippines often get hit by typhoons during certain months of the year.

Singapore sits near the equator, so we don't get typhoons ourselves - but many Singaporean families travel to Japan for holidays. Storms like this are a good reminder to check the weather before flights and trips.

lenses.me: If your family is planning a holiday to Japan, this is why parents always check typhoon warnings before booking flights.
lenses.family: Families with trips to Okinawa or nearby areas may need to change plans or keep a close eye on the news.
lenses.friends: You can share fun facts with your friends about how typhoons are like Singapore's thunderstorms, but much bigger and longer-lasting.
lenses.nation: Singapore doesn't get typhoons because we're near the equator, but we can still learn from how other countries prepare and stay safe.
lenses.world: Typhoons like Dolphin remind us that many parts of Asia face extreme weather that needs careful planning and safety measures.

stories.title: Singaporean Designer Turns Malay Treats into Beautiful Furniture
stories.headline_kid: A Singaporean designer named Faezah Shaharuddin makes furniture named after Malay desserts like Onde, Agar and Biskut!
summary: Faezah Shaharuddin runs a design studio in Singapore called Studio Kallang. Her furniture collections have sweet names like Onde, Agar and Biskut - names most Singaporeans would recognise as tasty Malay desserts and biscuits, not chairs or tables.

Faezah says her ideas come from her childhood, especially memories of watching skilled craftspeople work in furniture workshops across Southeast Asia. These experiences shaped what she calls her 'visual world' - the pictures and ideas in her mind that inspire her designs.

Each piece of furniture tells a story about Malay culture and heritage, mixing old traditions with fresh, modern shapes. It shows how everyday things from childhood, like favourite snacks, can spark big creative ideas.
Faezah's work celebrates Singapore's multicultural identity and puts Southeast Asian craft traditions on the map internationally, proving that stories from home can inspire world-class design.

lenses.me: It shows that things from your own childhood, like your favourite snacks, can inspire something creative and maybe even your dream job someday.
lenses.family: Your family might enjoy spotting the desserts these furniture pieces are named after next time you visit a Malay kueh stall.
lenses.friends: You could design your own 'furniture menu' inspired by your favourite snacks and imagine what shapes they'd take!
lenses.nation: Her work celebrates Singapore's Malay heritage and shows how our diverse cultures can inspire world-class design.
lenses.world: Studio Kallang's furniture is being noticed internationally, putting Singaporean and Southeast Asian craft traditions on the global stage.
